lesson.menu_title: I Used to Live in the City
lesson.menu_desc: Nobody decides their own habits -- they just happen, and then one day they are gone. Tonight, the three ways English talks about a routine that is over
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- I Used to Live in the City
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 10 -- I Used to Live in the City
lesson.grammar_point: used to and would for past habits

listenings.text: My name is Lars. I lived in Oslo for eighteen years and I moved out four years ago, and people always ask me what I miss. For a long time I said nothing, and that was not honest. What I miss is small. I used to walk down to the same coffee place every morning before seven, and the man there did not ask me what I wanted, he just started making it. That was second nature. I did not choose it. On Fridays my brother and I would meet at the station and take the last train together, and we never planned it once. Now I stock up on Saturday, I drive everywhere, and an errand takes half a day. Is it better? Yes. Do I miss the coffee man? Also yes. Both things are true, and nobody ever tells you that before you move.

I am Ruth, and I went the other way round. I grew up in a village in Yorkshire and I moved to London at twenty-six, and everybody expected me to talk about the traffic. What I actually noticed was the loss of the boring parts. At home I used to leave the house without locking the door, and I did not think about it, ever. Every Sunday my father and I would drive to the reservoir and say almost nothing for an hour. In London nothing is mundane in that way. Everything is a small decision, all day long. I do not want to go back, and I am not being sentimental. I am only saying that what I dreaded about moving was the noise, and what I actually lost was the part of the day where I was not deciding anything.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: Ordinary and repetitive, with nothing special about it
Something you do without thinking, after years of doing it
To stop somewhere quickly on your way to somewhere else
A small thing you do the same way every time, because it matters to you
A person who does the same things in the same order every day
Something small that takes far more effort than it should

vocab.text: Notice what these words are NOT about. Not one of them describes a decision. A ritual, second nature, a creature of habit: all three name something that happened to you without you ever choosing it. That is exactly why English gives past habits a grammar of their own.

reading.rtitle: The Habits You Only Notice When They Are Gone
paras: Ask anybody who has moved what changed, and they will tell you about the big things: the house, the drive, the noise. Ask the same person six months later and the answer is different. What changed was a dozen small rituals that nobody ever decided to have.

In a city, a life is built out of whatever is within walking distance. You used to stop at the same bakery because it was on the corner. Every Friday you would order takeout, because cooking after eleven hours was a hassle. None of that was a decision. It was second nature, and it disappeared in the week the corner stopped existing.

The countryside hands you a different set, and the new set is not automatically better. You stock up once a week because the shop is twenty minutes away. An errand that used to take four minutes now takes an afternoon. People who move imagine they are trading a busy life for a calm one. What they are really doing is trading one set of habits for another, and for about a year the new set feels mundane rather than peaceful.

English is unusually precise about all of this, and most learners use one third of it. Used to says the habit is over and is not true any more. Would puts the listener back inside a scene, but only when they already know which years you mean. The plain past is for the thing that happened once. The cost of using one form for everything is not grammatical: it is that the story flattens, and nobody can tell what you lost from what you did on a Tuesday.

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: How to choose between living in a city and living in the countryside
Moving changes a life through small automatic rituals, and English has three separate ways of talking about them
Why the countryside is calmer than the city

items: Six months later, people give the same answer about what changed.
The text says the answer is different the second time: the big things first, the small rituals only later.
The city rituals in the text were chosen on purpose.
It says none of that was a decision — it was second nature.
The text says country habits are automatically better than city ones.
It says the new set is not automatically better, and that for about a year it feels mundane rather than peaceful.
Would only works when the listener already knows which years you mean.
Used to says the habit is over; would puts the listener inside a scene, but only when the when is already on the table.
The text says the real cost of using one form for everything is grammatical.
It says the cost is that the story flattens and nobody can tell what you lost from what you did on a Tuesday.

items.situation: Somebody asks what you did every evening in the city that you do not do any more. Fifteen seconds.
tips: I used to order takeout three nights a week, because cooking after work was a hassle.
Used to opens a habit that is finished.

items.situation: Set a scene. One thing you did every Friday — and the listener already knows we are talking about your city years.
tips: Every Friday I would swing by the bakery on the way home.
Would needs the when to be on the table already.

items.situation: Say where you lived before, without using would.
tips: I used to live within walking distance of everything.
Live is a state. States take used to and never would.

items.situation: Name one thing you never did before and do every day now.
tips: I did not use to cook at all. Now I cook every night.
Did not use to — no d on the end of use.

items.situation: Ask a Norwegian colleague about her old routine in Oslo.
tips: Did you use to take the train, or did you drive?
The question is did you use to, never did you used to.

items.situation: One thing that happened once, with a year on it.
tips: I moved to the countryside in 2021.
One event with a number: plain past. Used to would be wrong here.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
key: The habit that is over: I used to order takeout three nights a week.
The scene, once the years are known: Every Friday I would swing by the bakery.
A state, so used to only: I used to live within walking distance of everything.
Never: I would live in the city · I would be a creature of habit · I would have a car.
The negative: I did not use to cook at all. No d on use.
The question: Did you use to take the train? Never did you used to.
The single event: In 2021 I moved to the countryside. Plain past, because it happened once.
And the one that is not grammar: a routine only sounds like a routine when you say how often it happened.
